questionText: What is the CLR, and what does the JIT compiler do?
shortAnswer: The CLR (Common Language Runtime) executes .NET code: it loads assemblies, JIT-compiles IL to machine code, manages memory (GC), enforces type safety, and handles exceptions. The JIT translates IL per method on first call (with tiered re-optimization for hot paths).
detailedAnswer: C# compiles to IL (Intermediate Language) + metadata in assemblies — platform-agnostic. At runtime the CLR: verifies type safety, JIT-compiles each method on first invocation (fast Tier0 with minimal optimization, then Tier1 optimized recompilation for hot methods via call counting — tiered compilation balances startup vs throughput), allocates/collects objects (GC), manages threads and AppDomains/AssemblyLoadContexts, throws and unwinds exceptions, and enforces security (CAS legacy, modern sandboxing via process boundaries). Related acronyms: CTS (Common Type System — the shared type rules enabling C#/F#/VB interop: every language's int is System.Int32), CLS (Common Language Specification — the subset guaranteed cross-language: avoid unsigned publics, case-only overload differences, to stay CLS-compliant). AOT alternative: Native AOT pre-compiles everything (no JIT, fast startup, bigger binaries, reflection limits). Diagnostics:DOTNET_Jit* env knobs, tiered compilation counters, and ReadyToRun (pre-JITed IL shipped in packages for faster startup).
internalWorking: Method entry points start as prestubs pointing at the JIT; first call triggers compilation (parse IL → IR → optimize → emit native + GC info/stack maps). Tier0→Tier1 promotion patches the entry (on-stack replacement for long-running loops). PGO (dynamic, .NET 7+) feeds runtime profiles back into optimization (devirtualization, inlining).
realWorldUsage: Startup tuning (ReadyToRun, tiered delays), warmup calls before load tests (promote Tier1 before measuring!), and AOT decisions for CLIs/containers.
commonMistake: Benchmarking cold Tier0 (always warm up — BenchmarkDotNet does), assuming IL runs interpreted (it never does — JIT or AOT), and shipping Debug builds to prod (no optimizations + extra checks).
technicalConversation: Ask why the first request is slower — Tier0 JIT + static constructors + cold caches is the full answer, and warmup strategy follows.
interviewFollowUp: How does tiered compilation balance startup versus steady-state throughput?
keyTakeaway: CLR = load + JIT + GC + safety. IL never runs directly; Tier0 starts fast, Tier1 optimizes hot.

questionText: What is an assembly, and what does it contain besides code?
shortAnswer: An assembly (.dll/.exe) is .NET's deployment unit: IL code + metadata (types, members, attributes) + manifest (identity, version, references) + resources. Strong-named assemblies add cryptographic identity for GAC/shared scenarios.
detailedAnswer: Contents: IL for all types, TypeDef/MemberRef metadata tables (enabling reflection without source), assembly manifest (name, version, culture, public key, referenced assemblies with versions — the binding contract), embedded resources (resx, our seed JSON!), and optionally native code (mixed-mode, ReadyToRun images). Identity = name + version + culture + public key token; the loader binds exact versions by default (binding redirects/roll-forward policies adjust). Versioning: AssemblyVersion (binding identity — change breaks consumers), FileVersion (informational), InformationalVersion (semver + commit hash — what --version shows). Loading: default context resolves from app dir + shared frameworks + NuGet cache; AssemblyLoadContext enables isolation (plugins unloadable — collectible contexts). Satellite assemblies hold localized resources per culture (fallback chain). Single-file publish bundles assemblies + runtime into one exe (extraction or in-memory load); Native AOT compiles to one native binary (no IL at all). Diagnostics: ildasm/ilspyc reflect contents; Fusion Log (bind failures on Framework; DOTNET_ tracing on Core).
internalWorking: The loader reads the manifest, resolves references (exact version → roll-forward rules), maps IL + metadata into memory, and JITs on demand. Strong-name verification is skipped by default on modern .NET (identity only, not security). Satellite probing: culture dir → parent cultures → neutral.
realWorldUsage: Plugin discovery (scan assemblies for IPlugin), embedded seed/config data, version diagnostics in health endpoints, and deployment packaging choices.
commonMistake: Version bumps breaking binding (AssemblyVersion churn — use FileVersion for builds), expecting satellite fallback to throw (it falls back silently), and Assembly.LoadFrom path hell (load contexts — LoadFrom ≠ Load, contexts matter).
technicalConversation: Ask how they would ship one exe — single-file (IL inside) vs Native AOT (native, limited reflection) is the trade-off conversation.
interviewFollowUp: Why do AssemblyVersion and FileVersion exist separately, and which breaks consumers when changed?
keyTakeaway: Assembly = IL + metadata + manifest + resources. Identity binds; versions communicate; contexts isolate.

questionText: What is the difference between the .NET SDK, runtime, targeting pack, and shared framework?
shortAnswer: SDK builds (compilers, tooling, templates); runtime executes (CLR + libraries on user machines); targeting pack provides compile-time reference assemblies; shared framework is the runtime's preinstalled library set apps roll forward to.
detailedAnswer: SDK (dotnet build/test/publish, e.g. 10.0.102): includes the latest runtime + targeting packs for supported versions — install on dev/CI. Runtime (Microsoft.NETCore.App, ASP.NET Core, WindowsDesktop): ships with apps (self-contained) or preinstalled on hosts (framework-dependent — small deployments, host controls patching). Targeting packs (ref assemblies in NuGet targeting packs): compile against APIs without implementing them (reference assemblies have signatures only — enables building for net8.0 on an SDK that runs net10). Shared framework: the machine-wide library set (C:\Program Files\dotnet\shared) — framework-dependent apps load from it (deduplication, centralized servicing). Roll-forward: patch/minor version policies (DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD=LatestMajor/Minor/Patch) decide version tolerance at startup. global.json pins the SDK per repo (rollForward policies for teams). TFMs (net10.0, net10.0-windows, netstandard2.0) declare API surface + OS binding. Self-contained vs framework-dependent publish: size/portability versus shared servicing (containers usually self-contained or runtime-image-based).
internalWorking: Build resolves reference assemblies (compile) → emits IL targeting the TFM; at run, host (dotnet.exe/apphost) locates the runtime per roll-forward rules, loads shared-framework assemblies (no app-local copies for framework deps), then JIT/AOT executes.
realWorldUsage: CI images (SDK), server/container runtimes (runtime images), library multi-targeting (net8.0 + net10.0), and version-pinning repos (global.json).
commonMistake: Building with the wrong SDK (global.json missing — 'works on my machine'), runtime missing on hosts (self-contained or runtime images fix), and netstandard confusion (libraries yes, apps no).
technicalConversation: Ask what ships to production from their pipeline — SDK on build agents, runtime-only images at deploy is the correct split.
interviewFollowUp: Why do reference assemblies exist separately from runtime assemblies?
keyTakeaway: SDK builds, runtime runs, targeting packs type-check, frameworks share. Pin SDKs, choose deployment per host.

questionText: How does .NET configuration layering work (appsettings, env vars, args, secrets)?
shortAnswer: Configuration stacks providers in order; later wins: appsettings.json → appsettings.{Env}.json → user secrets (dev) → environment variables → command line. Access via IConfiguration (string paths) or bound options (typed, validated).
detailedAnswer: Default host order: appsettings.json (base), appsettings.{Environment}.json (per-env overrides), User Secrets (dev-only, outside the repo), environment variables (containers/K8s — __ double-underscore nests: ConnectionStrings__Default), command line (--Key=Value, highest). Later providers override earlier per key (not deep-merge arrays — arrays replace wholesale!). Access: configuration["Section:Key"] or GetConnectionString("Default"); typed via builder.Services.Configure<MyOptions>(configuration.GetSection("My")) + IOptions<T>/Snapshot/Monitor injection. Reload: reloadOnChange:true + IOptionsMonitor/OnChange for hot config (IOptions<T> is singleton-frozen — restarts needed). Validation: ValidateDataAnnotations/ValidateOnStart (fail fast at boot, not first request). Secrets: never in JSON committed — User Secrets dev, Key Vault/env prod, file-mounts in K8s. Hierarchies: sections map to nested objects; bind lists carefully (index-keyed). Testing: MemoryConfigurationBuilder (in-memory dict) for deterministic config in tests.
internalWorking: Providers flatten to key-value pairs (colon-delimited); the configuration root merges by last-wins per key. Binding uses reflection + type converters (enums parse, TimeSpan parses, nested objects recurse). Change tokens fire reloads (file watchers + polling).
realWorldUsage: Per-env connection strings, feature flags, timeout tuning, secret injection in containers, and test overrides.
commonMistake: Array merge expectations (replace, not merge!), secrets in committed JSON, IOptions staleness (use Monitor for hot), and validating at first-use instead of startup (ValidateOnStart).
technicalConversation: Ask where their prod secrets live — env/KeyVault (good), committed JSON (incident), or 'the wiki' (worse).
interviewFollowUp: Why do arrays replace instead of merging across providers, and what breaks because of it?
keyTakeaway: Layered last-wins, typed + validated options, secrets out of repos. Arrays replace — plan for it.

questionText: What is the difference between IOptions, IOptionsSnapshot, and IOptionsMonitor?
shortAnswer: IOptions<T>: singleton, frozen at startup (config changes ignored). IOptionsSnapshot<T>: scoped, re-read per request (web apps). IOptionsMonitor<T>: singleton with current value + OnChange notifications (background services, hot reload). All wrap the same bound options; lifetime decides freshness.
detailedAnswer: IOptions<T>.Value computed once (first access, cached forever) — inject into singletons safely; config edits require restart. IOptionsSnapshot<T>.Value recomputed per scope (per HTTP request) — picks up reloadOnChange edits next request; scoped-only (injecting into a singleton captures one scope — captive misbehavior, use Monitor instead). IOptionsMonitor<T>.CurrentValue always fresh + OnChange(Action<T>) callbacks (reloadable singletons: cache managers, pollers adjusting intervals live). Named options: multiple sections bound by name (Configure<T>(name, section) + IOptionsMonitor.Get(name) / IOptionsSnapshot.Get(name) — multi-tenant/provider configs). Validation: ValidateOnStart works with all three (boot-time failure beats runtime surprises). Testing: Options.Create(new T {...}) fakes any of them (no config files in unit tests). Performance: Snapshot rebinds per request (small cost — fine; hot loops cache locally). Anti-pattern: IOptions<T> for values that change (stale), Snapshot in singletons (scope capture), Monitor without disposal of OnChange subscriptions (leak in long-lived hosts — hold the IDisposable).
internalWorking: OptionsManager caches per name (IOptions root); Snapshot uses scoped cache (per-scope recompute); Monitor holds a change-token subscription rebinding on reload events (file watcher → token fire → rebind + OnChange invoke).
realWorldUsage: Feature flags (Monitor), per-request tenant settings (Snapshot), static app constants (IOptions), and multi-provider configs (named).
commonMistake: Snapshot-in-singleton (stale scope capture), IOptions for hot values (restart required silently), and OnChange subscriptions never disposed (host-lifetime leak).
technicalConversation: Ask which lifetime their feature flags use — restart-required flags (IOptions) versus live flags (Monitor) is a deliberate product decision.
interviewFollowUp: How do named options work, and what scenario needs them?
keyTakeaway: IOptions = frozen singleton, Snapshot = per-request, Monitor = live + callbacks. Match lifetime to freshness needs.

questionText: How do configuration reload and change notifications work, and what are the pitfalls?
shortAnswer: File providers watch with reloadOnChange (debounced) and env vars poll; IOptionsMonitor rebinds + fires OnChange. Pitfalls: arrays replace wholesale, in-flight operations see mixed values, rapid saves flap, and non-file sources poll slowly (env vars ~15s+ in containers).
detailedAnswer: Mechanics: PhysicalFileProvider watches (debounce ~250ms) → ConfigurationReloadToken fires → bound options re-created → Monitor.OnChange invoked. Design for reload: read CurrentValue per operation (never cache in fields for hot values), make values atomic-consistent (related settings change together? version-stamp sections or accept transient mix), debounce reactions (rebuilding clients on every keystroke-save — throttle with a timer), and validate on reload too (Options validation runs per rebind with ValidateOnStart... actually per-change validation needs custom OnChange guards — invalid reloads can poison running state; validate before applying by staging). Env vars in containers: no file events (poll-based, slower — design for minutes, not seconds). K8s ConfigMaps: symlinked atomic swaps (watchers fire once per update — good). Secrets rotation: Key Vault provider polls (configure reload interval vs secret TTL). Testing reload: touch files in integration tests with waits (flaky by nature — generous timeouts, retry asserts). Non-reloadable realities: connection strings mid-flight (drain + recreate pools, don't hot-swap), thread-pool sizes (runtime-owned), and anything captured in closures (rebind points only).
internalWorking: ChangeToken abstraction (IChangeToken.HasChanged + callbacks); file watchers raise via PhysicalFilesWatcher (buffer overflows under rapid saves → missed events, another flapping source). OptionsMonitor caches per name, invalidates on token fire.
realWorldUsage: Log-level toggles, poll intervals, feature flags, downstream URLs, and rate limits adjusted without deploys.
commonMistake: Caching CurrentValue in fields (stale forever), reacting per-keystroke (flap storms), invalid reloads poisoning state (validate-then-apply), and undisposed OnChange subs (leak).
technicalConversation: Ask what happens mid-request when config flips — per-operation reads (consistent-ish) versus cached (stale) is the design line.
interviewFollowUp: Why can't you hot-swap a database connection string mid-flight, and what pattern replaces it?
keyTakeaway: Reload is file-watch + rebind + notify. Read per-operation, debounce reactions, validate before applying.

questionText: How do ILogger log levels and categories work, and what should you log at each level?
shortAnswer: Levels (Trace→Debug→Information→Warning→Error→Critical) filter by severity; categories (usually the class name) filter by source. Log: business milestones at Information, recoverable anomalies at Warning, failures needing action at Error, startup/shutdown + request summaries always, and Debug/Trace for dev-only detail.
detailedAnswer: Level guide: Trace (per-iteration/set-member detail — prod-off always), Debug (diagnostic flow — dev/test), Information (business events: order placed, user registered, seeding complete; request lines), Warning (recovered: retry succeeded, deprecated use, invalid input rejected, handled 404s), Error (failed operation needing attention: unhandled exceptions, DB down — with exception objects!), Critical (process/app-domain threatening: out of memory, data loss — triggers paging). Categories: ILogger<T> names after T (filter per namespace: Microsoft.AspNetCore → Warning, Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command → Information-in-dev). Filtering: appsettings Logging:LogLevel:Default + per-category overrides (our Serilog MinimumLevel.Override mirrors this). Costs: disabled levels must be cheap — guard expensive formatting (if (logger.IsEnabled(LogLevel.Debug)) or defer via structured params, never $"{Expensive()}" unconditionally — string interpolation evaluates eagerly!). Scopes: BeginScope with correlation/request ids (all logs in the operation carry it). Sinks: console (containers), files (rolling), Seq/AppInsights (queryable) — levels per sink (verbose file, warning+ remote).
internalWorking: IsEnabled checks level-vs-config first (nanoseconds when off); message templates parse once (cached) with named holes bound positionally (no boxing for value types via generic overloads — the performance story of modern logging). Scopes stack in AsyncLocal (flows across awaits).
realWorldUsage: Request logging (our UseSerilogRequestLogging), business audit trails, error alerting pipelines, and debug sessions via level toggles.
commonMistake: Eager interpolation (perf tax when off), logging PII/secrets/tokens (review every template!), Error without the exception object (stack lost), and Warning for business-as-usual (alert fatigue).
technicalConversation: Ask what their Error rate looks like — errors that never page are warnings wearing a costume; recalibrate levels by actionability.
interviewFollowUp: Why are structured templates cheaper than interpolation when the level is disabled?
keyTakeaway: Levels = actionability, categories = source. Structured params, scopes for correlation, never PII.

questionText: What is structured logging, and how does it change debugging versus string messages?
shortAnswer: Structured logging emits named properties (OrderId=42) alongside text, making logs queryable (filter/aggregate by field) instead of greppable strings. It changes debugging from reading lines to querying events — plus cheaper disabled-level paths.
detailedAnswer: String logging: $"Order {id} failed" bakes values into text (searchable only by substring, unaggregatable). Structured: LogError("Order {OrderId} failed: {Reason}", id, reason) preserves OrderId/Reason as fields — Seq/Datadog/AppInsights filter (OrderId=42), group (by Reason), and chart (failures/minute) over them. Conventions: PascalCase property names, stable names across call sites (OrderId everywhere — not Id/Order/orderId mixed), low-cardinality values in properties (never free text/tokens in fields — index explosion), exception objects as dedicated args (destructuring policies for custom types: Destructure.ByTransforming<Order>(o => new { o.Id, o.Total })). Scopes add ambient fields (RequestId, UserId — added once per operation). Costs: disabled levels skip rendering (cheap); enabled writes serialize (JSON sinks). Sinks: console JSON (containers → collectors), files (local), Seq (dev queryable), OTel (traces+logs correlated). Testing: in-memory sink asserting event presence/fields (not text matching!). Migration: replace interpolation site by site; lint for $" in Log* calls (custom analyzer or review checklist).
internalWorking: Templates parse to (text, property-tokens) once (cached per call site); rendering binds values positionally into LogEventProperty set (scalar/sequence/structure values). Sinks serialize properties (JSON) or format text. No boxing for common value types (generic overloads).
realWorldUsage: Seq/Datadog queries in incidents, alert grouping (by Reason/Endpoint), funnel analytics, and audit trails.
commonMistake: Interpolation (unqueryable + eager cost), inconsistent property names (unaggregatable), high-cardinality/PII in fields (index explosion + leaks), and destructuring entire aggregates (payload bombs — transform first).
technicalConversation: Ask them to find all failures for one order id — structured fields answer in seconds; string grep answers in minutes (or never).
interviewFollowUp: Why must property names be stable across call sites, and what breaks when they drift?
keyTakeaway: Log events with fields, not strings with values. Stable names, low cardinality, no PII.

questionText: What are Native AOT and ReadyToRun, and when should you choose each (or neither)?
shortAnswer: ReadyToRun pre-JITs IL into shipped binaries (faster startup, still needs runtime + allows JIT fallback). Native AOT compiles fully to native (no IL/JIT — fastest startup, smallest containers, but reflection/dynamic-code limits). Default JIT for servers; R2R for faster-start services; AOT for CLIs, lambdas, and tiny containers.
detailedAnswer: ReadyToRun (PublishReadyToRun): crossgen compiles IL ahead into native images inside the package — startup skips most JIT (cold-start wins 20–40%), runtime still present (JIT covers generics-over-unlisted-types and dynamic code; full flexibility retained). Costs: bigger binaries (~30%), publish-time CPU. Native AOT (PublishAot): full static compilation to one native exe (no dotnet runtime install, ms-scale startup, minimal memory) — constraints: no runtime codegen (Reflection.Emit, dynamic proxies/Moq, unannotated reflection over trimmed members fail — DynamicallyAccessedMembers annotations + source generators required), limited diagnostics (some profilers), longer publishes. Choose: long-running APIs → default JIT (peak throughput wins); CLI tools/serverless/edge → AOT (startup dominates); sized-up services wanting quicker warmup → R2R; libraries → neither (ship IL, let consumers decide — AOT-compatible code via annotations benefits everyone). Trimming (PublishTrimmed, subset of AOT tech) shrinks self-contained IL apps with the same reflection caveats. Testing AOT: publish + run integration tests against the native binary (behavioral deltas surface there, not in JIT test runs).
codeExample:
<!-- R2R: faster startup, full flexibility -->
<PublishReadyToRun>true</PublishReadyToRun>
<!-- AOT: native binary, constraints -->
<PublishAot>true</PublishAot>
<!-- Trim warnings as errors to catch AOT hazards early -->
<WarningsAsErrors>IL2026;IL2057;IL3050</WarningsAsErrors>
internalWorking: R2R embeds native code versioned per runtime (minimum-version binding, JIT fills gaps). AOT runs ILC (whole-program analysis → optimizing backend) with a closed-world assumption (all code visible at publish — hence dynamic-code limits). Trimming dataflows reachability from roots (Main + annotated members).
realWorldUsage: CLIs (dotnet-ef itself ships AOT-able), AWS Lambda cold starts, IoT/edge agents, and container slimming.
commonMistake: AOT + unannotated reflection (runtime MissingMetadata crashes), trim warnings ignored (publish succeeds, runtime fails), and AOT for throughput servers (JIT profiling beats static — measure, don't assume).
technicalConversation: Ask what dominates their profile: startup (AOT/R2R) or steady-state (JIT)? The answer picks the technology; most servers are steady-state.
interviewFollowUp: Why can't Native AOT support Reflection.Emit, and what replaces dynamic proxies there?
keyTakeaway: R2R = faster start, full .NET. AOT = native start, constrained code. Servers usually want JIT.

questionText: How do you manage secrets safely across dev, CI, and production?
shortAnswer: Dev: User Secrets (outside repo) + .gitignore vigilance. CI: masked pipeline variables / OIDC-fed short-lived credentials. Prod: managed identity + Key Vault (or env from orchestrator secrets), never files-in-repo or baked-in images. Rotate regularly; audit access.
detailedAnswer: Layers: (1) Code: no secret literals (analyzers + pre-commit hooks like gitleaks catch slips; revocation on leak, not just deletion — git history keeps it). (2) Dev: dotnet user-secrets (JSON outside the repo, per-user; team bootstrap scripts document required keys, never values). (3) CI: OIDC to cloud (no stored credentials — short-lived tokens), masked variables for the unavoidable, isolated secret scopes per environment. (4) Prod: managed identity (workload gets secrets without handling credentials — Azure Managed Identity / IRSA), Key Vault with rotation policies + reload-wired providers, K8s SealedSecrets/external-secrets (encrypted in git, decrypted in cluster). (5) Images: multi-stage builds excluding secrets (no COPY of .env, no ARG secrets persisting in layers — BuildKit secret mounts). Connection strings: Key Vault/env, never appsettings in prod (dev defaults only + missing-throw like ours). Rotation: versioned secrets + dual-support windows (old+new accepted during rollover), automated where possible. Telemetry: audit secret access (who/when), alert on anomalous reads. Incident: rotate, revoke, review logs for use, post-mortem the path in.
internalWorking: Providers poll/cache per TTL (Key Vault provider reload intervals balance freshness vs call cost/rate limits). Managed identity exchanges environment credentials for tokens via instance metadata (no secrets on disk). SealedSecrets decrypts in-cluster via controller-held keys.
realWorldUsage: Connection strings, API keys, certificates, signing keys, and third-party tokens across all environments.
commonMistake: Secrets in git (even 'temporarily'), .env copied into images (layer history!), long-lived CI credentials (use OIDC), and logging connection strings (our middleware/logs never do — verify yours).
technicalConversation: Ask where their prod DB password lives and who can read it — identity-based with audit trails is the mature answer.
interviewFollowUp: How do you rotate a database password with zero downtime?
keyTakeaway: Identity over credentials, vaults over files, rotation as routine. Leaks get revoked, not just deleted.
